result.summary: Nestor's tale of the Centaurs ends when Tlepolemus complains Hercules was left out, and Nestor bitterly recounts how Hercules killed his eleven brothers, including the shape-changer Periclymenus. Neptune then begs Apollo to avenge his son Cygnus, and Apollo guides Paris's arrow to kill Achilles, whose ashes and famous arms lead to the contest over them.

scenes.title: Nestor tells of Hercules
scenes.summary: Tlepolemus protests that Hercules is not praised, and Nestor reluctantly tells how Hercules destroyed Pylos, killed his brothers, and shot Periclymenus as an eagle. The feast then ends in sleep.
scenes.stakes: Nestor's old grief and hatred; Tlepolemus's honor as son of Hercules.

scenes.title: Neptune urges Apollo
scenes.summary: Neptune, still angry over Cygnus, asks Apollo to destroy Achilles by a secret arrow. Apollo, veiled in cloud, finds Paris and tells him to aim at Achilles.

scenes.title: Death of Achilles and his arms
scenes.summary: Achilles falls, is burned, and only his glory remains. His shield stirs a contest, and Agamemnon has the leaders judge it.
scenes.stakes: Achilles's fame and who will inherit his arms.

notable_quotes.reason: Achilles dies but his glory fills the world.
Poignant image of the great hero reduced to ashes.

analysis.text: Heroic fame outlasts the body, but divine grudges and vengeance shape human fates, even that of Achilles.
The Roman poet blends Homeric tradition with later legend, such as Apollo guiding Paris's arrow.

legacy.text: The phrase Achilles' heel for a fatal weakness derives from the tale of his one vulnerable spot.

fun_facts.text: Homer's Iliad does not narrate Achilles's death; Ovid draws on later tradition.

language_notes.text: Alcides is Hercules, named for his grandfather Alcaeus. The cloud-begotten monsters are the Centaurs, sons of Ixion and a cloud shaped like Juno.
The Pylian is Nestor, king of Pylos. Tlepolemus is a son of Hercules, so Nestor's silence about Hercules offends him.
Deiphobus, Polydamas and Hector were Trojan warriors. Nestor says Greeks do not praise enemies, so he likens Hercules to them.
The eagle carries Jove's thunderbolts, so it is the bird most pleasing to the king of the Gods.
The Tirynthian hero is Hercules, called after Tiryns, the city linked with his early life.
Nestor's rhetorical question is bitterly ironic: he claims he owes Hercules no praise, and addresses Tlepolemus as leader of the Rhodian fleet.
The gifts of Bacchus means wine; the guests resume drinking after the story.
Cygnus, son of Neptune, was invulnerable and killed by Achilles, who strangled him; Neptune turned him into a swan. 'Son of Sthenelus' refers to the swan's human namesake, another Cygnus.
Neptune and Apollo built Troy's walls for King Laomedon, who refused payment; hence 'in vain'. Smintheus is a title of Apollo.
'Delian God' is Apollo, born on Delos. He is Neptune's nephew, so 'uncle' fits.
The 'ravisher' is Paris, who abducted Helen, a Greek wife, and so caused the war.
Thermodontean battle-axe means the Amazons, who lived by the river Thermodon. Achilles had killed their queen Penthesilea.
Phrygians and Pelasgians mean Trojans and Greeks respectively, here used as poetic names.
The claimants are Diomedes (son of Tydeus), Ajax son of Oïleus, Menelaus, Ajax son of Telamon and Ulysses (son of Laërtes). Agamemnon is the elder Atreid.

context_notes.text: Hercules sacked Pylos, Nestor's city, in a campaign against Neleus, who had refused to purify him. Nestor was the youngest son and survived.
Neptune was the father of Neleus, so Periclymenus, Nestor's brother, received his shape-changing power from his grandfather.
Priam, king of Troy, had lost Hector to Achilles, so Achilles' death was his one consolation.
Agamemnon, descendant of Tantalus, commanded the Greek army and avoids deciding the dispute himself.

literary_notes.text: Nestor appears as a reluctant, aged storyteller, whose old grief and hatred surface when pressed.
Repeated crooked, hooked bill and talons make the eagle's attack vivid and violent.
The god-given power of transformation does not save Periclymenus; the arrow's pressure from his own falling weight drives it deeper.
Nestor calls his silence a form of revenge, a mild retaliation that is polite in tone yet pointed.
The narrator turns to address the dead Achilles directly, adding pathos and irony at his unheroic end.
The god who armed Achilles also destroyed him, since Apollo guided the arrow.
The great hero is reduced to ashes barely filling a small urn.
His small ashes are set against glory that fills the whole world, stressing that fame outlasts the body.
